Tomato_Healthy.description: Leaf exhibits uniform chlorophyll distribution, turgid cell structure, and no visible fungal spots or viral curling.
Tomato_Healthy.cause: Optimal growth conditions with balanced nutrients and irrigation.
treatments: Maintain consistent drip irrigation at the root zone (avoid wetting leaves).
Ensure proper crop spacing for air circulation and sunlight penetration.
Continue periodic scouting for early pest or disease symptoms.
Tomato_Healthy.organic_care: Apply compost tea or seaweed extract to strengthen natural plant immunity.

Tomato_Early_Blight.description: Dark brown to black concentric circular lesions ('target-board' pattern) with chlorotic yellow halos, starting on older foliage.
Tomato_Early_Blight.cause: Fungal pathogen favored by warm temperatures (24-29°C) and prolonged leaf wetness.
treatments: Apply protective copper-based fungicide (Copper Hydroxide) or Chlorothalonil upon first symptom onset.
Prune infected lower foliage immediately and burn/dispose away from the field.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; switch to drip irrigation.
Tomato_Early_Blight.organic_care: Spray Bacillus subtilis (Serenade) or copper octanoate organic bio-fungicide.

Tomato_Late_Blight.description: Large, irregular water-soaked pale-green to dark brown lesions. Rapidly blights foliage and stems during humid conditions.
Tomato_Late_Blight.cause: Water mold (Oomycete) favored by cool, wet weather (<20°C and >90% humidity). Notorious as the cause of the Irish Potato Famine.
treatments: Emergency application of systemic fungicides such as Mefenoxam or Mancozeb + Dimethomorph.
Strictly isolate infected plants; remove and bag severely damaged vines immediately.
Sterilize all pruning tools with 70% isopropyl alcohol between plants.
Tomato_Late_Blight.organic_care: Preventive copper sulfate applications; ensure wide row spacing to maximize airflow.

Tomato_Bacterial_Spot.description: Small, dark water-soaked spots (1-3mm) that turn angular and purplish-brown, often surrounded by yellow halos. Leaves may turn yellow and drop.
Tomato_Bacterial_Spot.cause: Bacterial infection transmitted by seed, infected crop debris, and splashing rain.
treatments: Spray Copper bactericide combined with Mancozeb (improves copper efficacy).
Avoid handling or cultivating plants when foliage is wet to prevent spreading bacteria.
Practice minimum 2-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops.
Tomato_Bacterial_Spot.organic_care: Apply Actinovate (Streptomyces lydicus) or Agri-Phage bacteriophage spray.

Tomato_Septoria_Leaf_Spot.description: Numerous small, circular lesions with dark brown margins and light tan or gray centers with tiny black fungal pycnidia dots inside.
Tomato_Septoria_Leaf_Spot.cause: Fungal spores overwintering in solanaceous weeds and crop debris, spread by wind-driven rain.
treatments: Apply Chlorothalonil, Pyraclostrobin, or Azoxystrobin fungicides at 7-10 day intervals.
Mulch heavily around the base of plants to prevent soil-splash onto lower leaves.
Prune bottom 12-18 inches of leaves to stop splash infection.
Tomato_Septoria_Leaf_Spot.organic_care: Neem oil or potassium bicarbonate sprays to suppress fungal sporulation.

Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl.description: Upward curling and cupping of leaf margins, severe interveinal chlorosis (yellowing), stunting, and aborted fruit set.
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl.cause: Begomovirus transmitted primarily by Silverleaf Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci).
treatments: Control whitefly vectors using systemic insecticides (Imidacloprid, Acetamiprid).
Install insect-proof fine mesh netting (50-mesh) in greenhouses and nurseries.
Rogue out and destroy infected viral plants immediately (viruses cannot be cured once inside the vascular system).
Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl.organic_care: Use yellow sticky traps to monitor whiteflies; spray insecticidal soap or horticultural neem oil weekly.
